Minimal example to inspect

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>HTML Paragraphs and Line Breaks</title>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>HTML Paragraphs and Line Breaks</h1>
    <p>Practice the concept in a small semantic document.</p>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

Run this as a baseline, then introduce duplicate input. Compare the new result with the baseline using browser developer tools; do not change several things at once or you will lose the cause of the difference.

How to decide whether to use it

Choose this approach when it expresses the requirement directly and the team can verify its behaviour. The main trade-off to discuss here is flexibility versus validation. If a simpler standard mechanism meets the same requirement, prefer the smaller solution and document why.

Before shipping, prefer a native feature before adding a dependency. This turns a code sample into an engineering decision that another person can maintain. For html paragraphs, apply this check to the exact behaviour shown in the example above.

Debugging checklist for html paragraphs

  1. Confirm the input, selector, key, path or identifier is the value you think it is.
  2. Inspect the runtime or browser state immediately before the failing step.
  3. Reduce the case until the problem still appears with the fewest moving parts.
  4. Test duplicate input explicitly instead of assuming the happy path covers it.
  5. Write down what fixed the issue so the same regression can be tested later.

Practice challenge

Add this concept to a classroom exercise, but change the example enough that copying is impossible. Include one normal case, one duplicate input case and one deliberate error. Explain which observation from browser developer tools told you the implementation was correct.

For a second pass, replace one design choice and compare flexibility versus validation. Your explanation of that comparison is more valuable than producing a larger snippet.

What you should be able to explain

  • What html paragraphs is responsible for.
  • Which input or state controls its behaviour.
  • How you would verify the result with browser developer tools.
  • What changes when duplicate input occurs.
  • When a simpler alternative would be easier to maintain.

Finally, review HTML Paragraphs and Line Breaks from the perspective of the next maintainer.
